newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Despite Taleban, women are back working.
newsitem.headline: Despite Taleban, women are back working.

text.p: In a compound in the heart of Kabul, 250 women were busy weaving carpets, blankets and turban cloths on Wednesday despite an edict from the Taleban authorities that women should stay at home.
"When the Taleban came to Kabul, the project closed for two days," explains one of the male overseers, Solih Mohammed. "Then the women went to see them and asked for permission to re-open it."
"When I went there I took a letter with the thumb prints of all the women on it," said Nasima, one of the women who confronted the purist Islamic Taleban.

"I told them we were very poor and that we don't have men to work for us. I told them that if they closed the project they would have to give us food, and then I said that even if they didn't give us permission, we would come to work anyway."
"After two or three visits they gave us a letter saying we could carry on," she said with a smile.
The women are mostly widows and work in a vocational training project funded partly by the World Food Programme (WFP) and partly by the money made from selling their products.
When the Taleban took Kabul on September 27, they told women they should only leave home wearing the all-enveloping burqa, a shroud-like veil that leaves only a small patch of gauze to see out of.
Solih Mohammed said the project's line in turban cloths had been particularly successful since the Taleban take-over.

At work, none of the women wear the burqa, taking them off after travelling to the compound. Chiqeba, a 30-year-old wearing a black and red dress with gold buttons and a light head scarf, said she was beaten by the Taleban shortly after their arrival for being improperly dressed.

"I was traveling in a bus when some Taleban pulled me off and beat me for not wearing a burqa," she said. "It cost me 500,000 Afghanis ($33 dollars) to buy one. I had to sell a pair of ear-rings to raise the money."
She is now paid 200,000 Afghanis ($13 dollars) a month and some wheat flour while learning to weave patous, the blanket that for most Afghan men takes the place of overcoats.
Razia, a 19-year-old who was a student and part-time medical receptionist until the Taleban closed her high school, said her job on the project provides the only income for her family.
"My father disappeared in the war, my mother was wounded in a rocket attack and my brother and sister are too young to work," she said.
The vocational training project is just one example of how the Taleban are gradually softening their line, if not their rhetoric, on women's employment.
Many of the women staff of aid agencies in Kabul are back at work with the tacit permission of the Taleban.
The Taleban have also allowed some female medical staff to resume their jobs, but only under strict guidelines.

There are still many more women who are not allowed to go to work. "A month ago I was a teacher of literature in a high school," said one burqa-clad woman in a Kabul street asking for money. "Now I am a beggar. Tell the world we cannot survive like this."

Even among the few women who are still working, the Taleban's rule is not popular. "I am not happy they have come here because they don't want us to be free," said one project worker who didn't want to give her name.
Kabul is an island of relative modernity in Afghanistan and the Taleban's puritanical vision of Islam sits ill with the majority of its cosmopolitan population.

The number of men either killed or otherwise unavailable for employment because of the war meant that women had won a major role in the life of Kabul, over-riding a tradition that said women should not work.

At the vocational training project, sitting at their looms in the courtyard and protected from the autumn sunshine by tarpaulins, the women laugh and stare boldly at the foreigner asking them questions. They remain uncowed by the Taleban.
